input_text:
Nobody in the village of Hollow Creek could say who had built the chapel on the marsh path, only that it was already old when the oldest grandmother was young. Its door opened only on foggy evenings, and whoever stepped inside to shelter found the candles already burning, though no one ever saw them lit. Travelers learned to hurry past it before dusk, for the bell sometimes rang by itself, low and patient, like a call meant for one particular soul. Those who stopped to listen said the sound followed them home and lodged behind the ribs, tolling again whenever they lied. The priest at the village church forbade any talk of it, yet kept a sprig of rosemary nailed above his own door. Even the skeptics who mocked the story kept their shutters latched a little tighter than before.

When I was twelve, my friend Dara vanished on the marsh path on the evening of the harvest fair. Search parties found her ribbon caught on a thorn bush and her shoes set neatly side by side, pointed toward the chapel. The door stood shut and the dust inside lay undisturbed. Her mother lit a candle in the window every night for seven years. The flame itself seemed to answer, bending toward the marsh as if someone had called her name. On the eighth year the candle guttered out at midnight, and in the morning the villagers found the chapel door ajar, a child-sized handprint fading on the wood. Dara never came back, but her mother said she had heard her laughing inside, and that was enough.

Years later, a surveyor came from the city to map the marsh for a new road, scoffing at our stories over ale at the inn. He camped by the chapel on his third night, claiming ghosts did not trouble men with instruments and ledgers. At dawn we found his theodolite toppled, his maps scattered in the water, and the man himself sitting on the chapel steps with his hair gone white. He never said what had come to him in the fog. But he paid the innkeeper, burned his maps, and took the first coach out, leaving the road unbuilt for another twenty years. After that, even the skeptical learned to cross themselves when the bell began to toll.

The chapel did not only take; sometimes it gave things back, though never in the way anyone wished. A farmer who lost his wedding ring in the marsh found it on his pillow the next morning, still cold as river water. A widow who prayed there for her drowned son began finding wet footprints on her stairs. The footprints climbed every night for a month, pausing outside her door, until she finally opened it and found only a pile of river weed and her son's wooden whistle. She kept it anyway, and on quiet nights the neighbors swear they hear it play, thin and sweet, from somewhere beneath her floorboards.

My grandmother warned me never to answer if the chapel called me by name, for names are the doors we open ourselves. One foggy autumn evening I heard mine, soft and familiar, spoken in my mother's voice, though my mother had been dead three winters. I stood frozen on the path while the candles flared inside and the bell held its breath, waiting. Something in me wanted to answer more than I have ever wanted anything, but I remembered her rule and bit my tongue until it bled. The voice called twice more, each time gentler, and when I did not answer it sighed, the candles went out together, and the fog rolled back like a curtain closing.

They say the chapel chooses, and that what it takes it keeps, and that the fog is only its breath moving over the marsh. Whether that is true, no one can say, but the road was never built. The bell still tolls on damp evenings. Every year on the night of the harvest fair a candle appears in a window of the oldest house in the village. Nobody admits to lighting it. The house has stood empty since Dara's mother died, her last candle burned down to a puddle of wax beside a wooden whistle nobody dares to touch. And on foggy evenings, if you stand very still on the marsh path, you can hear it play, and you will understand why we hurry home before dusk.
